title: Scale from Zero to Millions of Users
problem: Evolve a single-server web app into a multi-tier, multi-region architecture that serves millions of users with low latency and high availability.
summary: A canonical read-heavy web application (about 10:1 read/write). We take the mature end-state that; an L7 load balancer terminates TLS and spreads traffic across a stateless web tier; session state is evicted from the web tier into a shared NoSQL store so any server can handle any request (enabling autoscaling); a Redis cache absorbs the hot read set; the SQL store is split into a master for writes and slave replicas for reads; a CDN fronts static assets; a message queue decouples slow work (photo processing, emails) to asynchronous worker pools; the data tier ultimately shards by user id; logging/metrics/automation run across everything. The dominant tradeoff is consistency vs latency — reads from replicas and CDN edges can be seconds stale, so write paths must invalidate cache entries and accept replica lag on subsequent reads.

functional: Serve HTTP requests for a read-heavy web workload with roughly a 10:1 read/write ratio
Support user signup, login, and session-backed authenticated browsing
Return personalised content whose hot working set fits comfortably in cache
Upload and serve user-generated media through a CDN-fronted object store
Offload slow work (thumbnailing, transactional email, push) to asynchronous workers
Expose health and readiness endpoints for the orchestrator and load balancer
Provide per-request and per-service metrics plus centralized logs for operators
nonFunctional: Availability target of 99.99% for the read path, 99.9% for the write path
p99 read latency under 200 ms at the edge, under 50 ms for cache hits
Horizontal scale from one instance to thousands without code changes
Survive the loss of an entire availability zone with no data loss
Cost scales sub-linearly with traffic thanks to caching and CDN offload
No single stateful component is a hard SPOF once past the MVP stage

assumptions: Session/profile row ~2 KB; hot working set ~20% of users
99.95% monthly availability target (≈ 22 min/month downtime budget)
estimates: Cache working set: 5M * 20% * 2 KB ≈ 2 GB (fits comfortably in a single Redis node; use a 3-node replicated cluster for HA)
Primary DB write load ≈ 500 QPS peak — well within a single well-tuned Postgres/MySQL primary before sharding is needed
Static asset egress via CDN offloads ~80% of bytes — origin bandwidth bill drops ~5x
Async job volume (photo resize, email send, etc.) ~200/s off the synchronous path into the message queue; worker pool sized for ~2x burst absorption
Multi-DC geoDNS split: ~60/40 US-East / US-West in steady state; 100% to survivor on DC outage

architecture.mermaid: graph LR client[Client] --> dns[DNS] client --> cdn[CDN] dns --> lb[Load Balancer] lb --> web[Web Tier] web --> cache[(Redis Cache)] web --> session[(Session Store)] web --> dbprimary[(DB Primary)] web --> dbreplica[(DB Replica)] web --> mq[[Message Queue]] mq --> worker[Worker Pool] dbprimary --> dbreplica

client.name: Client (Browser / Mobile)
client.summary: Browser or native app that resolves DNS, fetches static assets from the CDN, and calls the API for dynamic content.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Resolve `app.example.com` via DNS (TTL 60s for failover)
- Load static JS/CSS/images from the CDN host
- Call `api.example.com` for dynamic reads/writes
- Hold session cookie / JWT; retry idempotent GETs with backoff

sections.heading: Why DNS matters here
sections.body: A short TTL lets operators point users at a healthy region in minutes during a regional outage. Long TTLs (1h) save DNS load but tie users to a dead region until cache expires.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: Every millisecond shaved on the client side (keepalive, HTTP/2, TLS session resumption) is a millisecond you don't have to squeeze out of the backend. The client is where latency budgets start.

bottlenecks.title: Stale DNS resolver pins users to a dead region
bottlenecks.trigger: During a regional outage, despite the 60s TTL on app.example.com, intermediate resolvers (ISPs, corporate) often ignore TTLs and cache A records for 5–30 minutes, stranding a slice of the 5M DAU on the failed region's LB IP.
bottlenecks.symptom: A fraction of users see connection timeouts or TLS failures for minutes after DNS failover has already pointed healthy users elsewhere; regional error rate doesn't converge to zero after failover.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Ship a client-side health probe + fallback: app tries api.example.com, on N consecutive failures retries against a secondary hostname (api-west.example.com) with its own DNS entry. For native apps, bypass OS resolver with a DNS-over-HTTPS client and honor the 60s TTL directly.
bottlenecks.detection: Compare regional error rates after a forced failover drill; alert if per-region 5xx/connection-error rate stays >1% more than 90s past the DNS TTL window. Track client-reported resolved-IP in RUM telemetry.

bottlenecks.title: TLS handshake + connection churn on cold starts
bottlenecks.trigger: At ~20 page views/user/day many sessions are short; without HTTP/2 keep-alive and TLS session resumption, each cold request pays ~100–300ms for TCP+TLS, easily consuming the entire 200ms p95 budget before the backend is even touched.
bottlenecks.symptom: p95 end-to-end latency exceeds 200ms target on mobile/lossy networks even though backend timings (hot cache hit ~10ms) look healthy; RUM shows large 'connection' and 'ssl' timing buckets.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce HTTP/2 (or HTTP/3/QUIC at the CDN+LB), enable TLS 1.3 with 0-RTT resumption, serve a Strict-Transport-Security header with preload, and use <link rel=preconnect> to api.example.com and the CDN origin from the initial HTML.
bottlenecks.detection: Browser RUM (Navigation Timing API): alert when p95 of connectEnd-connectStart or secureConnectionStart-connectStart exceeds 50ms for >5% of sessions; monitor HTTP/2 adoption ratio at the LB.

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded client retries amplify backend load during incidents
bottlenecks.trigger: Clients retry idempotent GETs with backoff; during a partial outage (e.g., Redis cold start, replica lag spike), 5M DAU retrying in lockstep can turn the normal 5K peak read QPS into a 15–25K QPS thundering herd.
bottlenecks.symptom: After a brief backend hiccup, traffic does not recover smoothly — instead QPS spikes 3–5x and the web tier (3000 concurrency cap) saturates, cascading into DB primary write queue and extending the incident.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement jittered exponential backoff (base 500ms, cap 30s, full jitter), cap retries at 3, honor Retry-After headers, and use a circuit breaker in the client SDK that trips after 5 consecutive failures for 10s. For native apps, coalesce duplicate in-flight GETs by URL.
bottlenecks.detection: At the LB, alert when the ratio of retried-requests (identified via Idempotency-Key or client-generated request-id repeats) exceeds 10% of total, or when QPS rises >2x while unique-session count is flat.

prebuild.explanation: ### Why the client is called out here In most system design diagrams the client is drawn as a box and then ignored — but at the scale this design targets, the client is where your latency budget starts bleeding. The problem statement fixes a **p95 end-to-end latency of 200ms globally**. That's not 200ms of backend time — it's 200ms from the moment the user's finger leaves the screen until pixels change. DNS lookup, TCP handshake, TLS handshake, and request serialization all happen on the client before your load balancer has seen a single byte. For a read-heavy app serving 5M DAU across multiple regions, ignoring the client means the backend could be perfect and users would still feel the app is slow. ### What happens without treating the client as a real component Concretely: if the client doesn't reuse TLS sessions or HTTP/2 connections, every page view pays ~100–300ms for connection setup on mobile networks. The operator sees healthy backend metrics (cache hits in 2ms, DB in 5ms) but RUM telemetry shows p95 at 400ms+. Worse, if the client retries aggressively on failure without jittered backoff, a brief Redis hiccup turns into a thundering herd — the web tier's 3000-concurrency cap saturates and the DB primary queues writes. ### The numbers At 5M DAU × 20 page views/day = **100M page views/day**, averaging ~1,160 QPS but peaking at 5K QPS. If even 10% of those clients retry once during a 30-second glitch, that's 5,000 × 0.1 × 30 = **15,000 extra requests** piled onto a recovering system. Client-side backoff isn't optional at this scale — it's load-shedding. ### Trade-off Pushing logic (retry policy, connection reuse, DNS fallback) into the client means you now ship and version that logic across browsers and native apps, which is harder to fix than a server-side deploy.

dns.name: DNS (Route53 / Cloud DNS)
dns.summary: Geo-aware DNS that returns the closest healthy region's load-balancer IP.

sections.heading: Routing policy
sections.body: Geolocation or latency-based routing + health checks. A failing region is pulled from rotation within 30–60s once its health check crosses threshold.

sections.heading: TTL choice
sections.body: 60s TTL on A records balances fast failover against DNS lookup volume. Some CDN providers recommend 20s for aggressive failover.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- DNS provider outage is existential; use a secondary provider for critical zones.
- A stale resolver somewhere in the internet can pin a user to a dead region for minutes regardless of your TTL.

gained: Full control over records and routing logic
lost: Must operate a global anycast fleet yourself
Harder to integrate managed health checks

bottlenecks.title: Resolver TTL disobedience strands users during regional failover
bottlenecks.trigger: Despite the 60s TTL on app.example.com, many ISP and corporate resolvers cache A records for 5–30 minutes. When the geo health check pulls a failed region in 30–60s, a meaningful slice of the 5M DAU (potentially hundreds of thousands of users in the affected region) keeps resolving to the dead LB IP.
bottlenecks.symptom: Regional 5xx/connection-error rate fails to drop to zero minutes after the DNS failover; support tickets spike from a subset of ISPs/enterprises while other users on the same continent are fine. The 99.95% / 22-min-per-month availability budget is burned in a single incident.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Layer client-side fallback (native app DoH client honoring 60s TTL; web app retries api-west.example.com after N failures on api.example.com) on top of DNS, and combine with anycast LB VIPs so the IP itself can be moved without a DNS change. Keep TTL at 60s (do not go to 20s — see next bottleneck).
bottlenecks.detection: Run quarterly forced-failover drills and alert if per-region connection-error rate stays >1% for more than 90s past the TTL window. Track resolved-IP distribution in RUM telemetry; alert when >0.5% of sessions resolve to a drained region 5 minutes post-failover.

bottlenecks.title: DNS provider outage is a hard single point of failure
bottlenecks.trigger: A single managed DNS provider (Route53, Cloud DNS) going down — as happened to Dyn in 2016 — makes app.example.com unresolvable globally regardless of how healthy the regions, LBs, and web tier are. With 100M page views/day this translates to ~1.16M unresolvable page views per minute of outage.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users see NXDOMAIN or SERVFAIL; the site appears completely down while internal dashboards (which resolve via cached or internal DNS) show green. New sessions cannot start; existing sessions on keep-alive connections keep working briefly, masking the scope.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Dual-provider DNS for the apex zone (e.g., Route53 + NS1 or Cloudflare as secondary) with zone transfers/automation keeping records in sync. Publish NS records for both providers so resolvers fall through on SERVFAIL. Keep zone records minimal and automate sync via Terraform or octoDNS.
bottlenecks.detection: External synthetic DNS probes from multiple continents and resolvers (e.g., Catchpoint, ThousandEyes) alerting on NXDOMAIN/SERVFAIL >0.1% over 60s. Monitor the provider's status page via API and alert on degraded state independently of query success.

bottlenecks.title: Aggressive TTL shortening amplifies query volume and cost
bottlenecks.trigger: Operators tempted to cut TTL from 60s to 20s (per some CDN vendor guidance) for faster failover will ~3x the DNS query rate. With 5M DAU opening multiple sessions per day across multiple domains (app, api, CDN origin), query volume can jump from low tens of millions/day into the hundreds of millions/day, raising Route53 bills and pressuring per-account query quotas.
bottlenecks.symptom: DNS bill spikes 3–5x after a TTL change; resolver query latency p95 creeps up (more cache misses at ISP resolvers); on heavy-traffic days, query throttling by the managed DNS provider produces intermittent SERVFAIL.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Keep TTL at 60s as the design specifies; achieve fast failover via client-side fallback and anycast IPs rather than ever-shorter TTLs. If sub-60s failover is truly needed, use health-checked anycast (IP-level failover, 0s effective TTL) instead of cutting DNS TTL further.
bottlenecks.detection: Track daily DNS query count and $/day trendline; alert on >50% week-over-week growth not explained by DAU growth. Monitor resolver cache-hit ratio via passive DNS or provider analytics; alert if hit ratio drops below 70%.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why DNS is here for *this* problem The design goal is **multi-region** service for 5M daily users with a **p95 latency budget of 200ms globally** and **99.95% availability**. That combination forces a decision on the very first hop: when a user in Frankfurt types your hostname, *which region's load balancer do they talk to?* A plain DNS record that always returns "US-East LB" means European users eat a 150ms transatlantic round trip before your load balancer even sees the packet — you've blown the latency budget at step zero. Geo-aware DNS with health checks is the mechanism that sends each user to the nearest *healthy* region, and pulls a dead region out of rotation within 30–60s so the availability budget survives a data-center outage. ## What happens without it Without geo-routed DNS, you'd either hard-code one region (fast for locals, slow for everyone else) or round-robin across regions (half your users get a slow region at random). Worse, when US-East goes down, every user keeps resolving to its dead IP — the operator sees connection timeouts climbing, the US-West LB sits idle with spare capacity, and there's no automatic way to shift traffic. You'd be manually editing DNS records during an incident while your error budget bleeds out. ## The numbers At 100M page views/day ≈ 1,160 QPS average with 3–5× peaks (~5K QPS), a 30-second manual failover wastes ≈ **150,000 requests**. A 60s-TTL health-checked DNS cut-over wastes ≈ 60s × 5,000 = **300K requests worst case**, but it happens automatically — no human in the loop at 3am. ## The trade-off Short TTLs (60s) mean more DNS query volume and cost, and you still can't force misbehaving resolvers to honor them — so DNS is necessary but not sufficient for fast failover.

cdn.name: CDN (CloudFront / Cloudflare)
cdn.summary: Global edge cache serving static and semi-static assets close to users.

sections.heading: What's cached
sections.body:
- Static: JS bundles, CSS, fonts, images (cache-key = URL, TTL = 1y with content hashing)
- Semi-static: public profile images, product catalogue JSON (TTL = 5m, stale-while-revalidate)
- Dynamic API calls are NOT cached — they fall through to the LB

sections.heading: Cache behavior
sections.body: On miss, the edge POP pulls from origin (the web tier) and caches with the origin's `Cache-Control` header. Popular objects are hot in 100+ POPs globally within seconds.

sections.heading: Why CDN before scaling the web tier
sections.body: Moving static bytes out of the origin drops origin egress 5–10x and lets one origin serve many more dynamic QPS.

lost: Less AWS-native integration than CloudFront
Log/analytics pipeline different from the rest of your AWS stack

gained: VCL lets you program edge logic like a real language
lost: Smaller footprint than Cloudflare
Higher $/GB at low scale

bottlenecks.title: Origin shield stampede on cache miss / invalidation
bottlenecks.trigger: A popular asset (e.g., a new JS bundle deploy or a purged product-catalogue JSON with 5m TTL) simultaneously misses at many of the 100+ edge POPs. With 5M DAU pulling ~20 page views/day and ~80% of bytes normally served from CDN, a cold deploy can fan in thousands of concurrent origin pulls to the web tier (concurrency cap 3000) within seconds.
bottlenecks.symptom: Web tier CPU spikes and p95 jumps from ~10ms to hundreds of ms; LB queue depth climbs; some edge POPs return 502/504 during the fill window; global error rate briefly breaches the 99.95% budget.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable origin shield / tiered caching (CloudFront Origin Shield, Cloudflare Argo Tiered Cache, Fastly shielding POP) so only one mid-tier POP pulls from origin per object. Use content-hashed URLs for JS/CSS (TTL=1y, never invalidated) and `stale-while-revalidate`/`stale-if-error` on semi-static JSON so misses serve stale while one request refills.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when origin request rate > 20% of edge request rate for >60s, or when origin 5xx rate exceeds 0.5%. Track cache-hit ratio per POP in CDN logs; page on-call if global hit ratio drops below 90% (normal ~98%).

bottlenecks.title: Cache-key explosion from query strings and Vary headers
bottlenecks.trigger: Analytics/marketing query params (utm_source, fbclid, gclid) and `Vary: Accept-Encoding, User-Agent` cause otherwise-identical assets to be cached as distinct objects. At 100M page views/day, a single shared image keyed naively on full URL can balloon to millions of cache entries, dropping hit ratio and inflating origin egress back toward the pre-CDN baseline (5–10x bill increase).
bottlenecks.symptom: Cache-hit ratio drifts down from ~98% toward 80–85%; origin bandwidth and web-tier QPS creep up week-over-week with no DAU growth; CDN storage/egress bill rises faster than traffic.
bottlenecks.mitigation: At the CDN, normalize cache keys: strip tracking query params (CloudFront cache-key policy allowlist; Cloudflare Cache Rules; Fastly VCL `req.url = querystring.filter_except(...)`). Vary only on `Accept-Encoding`; never on `User-Agent`. Serve images via a canonical path with explicit size/format variants instead of UA sniffing.
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor unique-cache-key count per asset prefix; alert when it grows >2x week-over-week. Track hit ratio by content-type and alert if HTML/JSON hit ratio drops below 90% or image hit ratio below 95%.

bottlenecks.title: Stale purge / invalidation lag after a bad deploy
bottlenecks.trigger: A broken JS bundle or wrong product-catalogue JSON is pushed; CloudFront invalidations typically take 60–300s to propagate across 100+ POPs, and during that window up to 5K peak QPS worth of users continue to receive the bad asset from edge caches.
bottlenecks.symptom: Rollback deploy completes on the origin but user-reported errors persist for minutes; RUM shows mixed old+new bundle versions in flight; support tickets for 'blank page' or 'stale prices' continue after the fix is 'live'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use content-hashed filenames for all immutable assets (app.[hash].js) so a rollback is a pointer swap in the HTML, not a purge. For semi-static JSON, prefer Fastly-style instant (sub-second) surrogate-key purges or Cloudflare cache-tag purges over URL-based invalidation. Keep a tested emergency purge runbook and rehearse it quarterly.
bottlenecks.detection: Synthetic probes from multiple POPs fetching known-bad URLs after a purge; alert if the old `ETag`/content-hash is still observed >120s post-purge. Track deploy→global-consistency time as an SLI; alert if it exceeds 5 minutes.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a CDN is here for *this* problem The problem is a multi-region app serving 5M DAU with a **p95 latency budget of 200ms globally**. A huge fraction of every page view is bytes that never change per user — JS bundles, CSS, fonts, product images. If every one of those bytes has to travel from your origin region to a user in Singapore, you've already blown the latency budget on static content alone, and your origin bandwidth bill is paying for traffic that is byte-for-byte identical across millions of users. The CDN exists to move those bytes to ~100+ edge POPs close to users, so the only thing that has to cross oceans is the small, personalized API response. ## What happens without it Without the CDN, every image and JS bundle hits your load balancer and web tier directly. The web tier's 3000-concurrency cap gets chewed up serving static bytes instead of dynamic API calls; p95 latency climbs for users far from the origin region; and your egress bill from the cloud provider balloons. Operators see web-tier CPU spiking during traffic peaks even though the DB and cache look fine — because the servers are busy shoveling the same logo PNG to a million browsers. ## The numbers At **100M page views/day**, CDN offload of ~80% of bytes means the origin only serves the remaining 20%. That's a **5× reduction in origin egress** — turning a potential 5 Gbps sustained origin load into ~1 Gbps, and freeing the web tier's 5K peak QPS to be spent on actual dynamic work. ## Trade-off You accept that cached content can be seconds-to-minutes stale globally, and that purging a bad deploy takes 60–300s to propagate across every POP.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 load balancer terminating TLS and spreading dynamic traffic across stateless web replicas.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Round-robin with least-connections fallback on the healthy pool. Health checks every 5s on `/healthz`; eject after 3 consecutive 5xx inside 10s.

sections.heading: TLS termination
sections.body: Terminates TLS once at the LB; plaintext HTTP inside the VPC. Saves ~3–5ms per request vs re-encrypting to the web tier.

sections.heading: HA
sections.body: Deploy as a managed service (AWS ALB, GCP L7 LB) which is itself redundant across AZs. The LB is the doorway — if it's down, the whole region is down.

gained: Full config control (rewrite rules, custom Lua)
Runs on any cloud or bare metal
lost: You own the HA story (keepalived / VIPs)
Capacity planning is your problem
Control plane is extra moving parts
Slightly higher per-hop CPU than NGINX

bottlenecks.title: LB is the regional single point of failure / blast radius
bottlenecks.trigger: The LB fronts 100% of dynamic traffic for its region (up to 5K peak read QPS + 500 write QPS). A control-plane misconfig (bad listener rule, expired TLS cert, security-group change) or a managed-service AZ-level incident takes the doorway down — even though web/DB/cache are healthy, the region is effectively offline.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sudden cliff in regional traffic to zero while backend dashboards show no load; external synthetics fail TLS handshake or get connection-refused; 99.95% monthly budget (22 min) burns in a single event since DNS failover still needs 30–60s to pull the region.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy the LB as a managed multi-AZ service (ALB/GCP L7) with at least 2 AZs active; keep an identical LB stack in the peer region with geo-DNS health checks so cross-region failover happens in 30–60s; automate TLS cert rotation via ACM/cert-manager with 30-day expiry alerts; gate LB config changes behind staged rollout (canary listener) and Terraform plan review.
bottlenecks.detection: External synthetic probes from 3+ geos hitting `/healthz` every 10s with alert on 2 consecutive failures; CloudWatch/GCP metric on LB `HTTPCode_ELB_5XX_Count` > 1% of requests over 1 min; cert-expiry alert at 30/14/7 days; alarm on `HealthyHostCount` = 0 in any AZ.

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU saturates under handshake storms
bottlenecks.trigger: At 5K peak QPS with ~20 page views/user/day, many sessions are short and pay full TLS handshakes. A retry storm (per the client component's bottleneck) or a forced cross-region failover can spike new-connection rate 3–5x to ~15–25K handshakes/s — TLS termination is CPU-bound (RSA/ECDSA ops ~1–5ms each) and the LB's effective concurrency (50K) is throttled by CPU before connection count.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegs at 100% while backend web tier sits idle; p95 latency jumps 50–200ms purely in the TLS layer; `TargetConnectionErrorCount` stays low but `ClientTLSNegotiationErrorCount` rises; RUM shows bloated `secureConnectionStart` timings consuming most of the 200ms budget.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce TLS 1.3 with session resumption (0-RTT) and HTTP/2 multiplexing so 1 TCP+TLS handshake carries many requests; prefer ECDSA certs over RSA (~5x faster handshakes); enable ALB's built-in session cache; pre-provision LB capacity (AWS pre-warming request) ahead of known traffic events; offload static asset TLS to the CDN (already designed) so only dynamic API traffic hits the LB.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when LB CPU > 70% for 2 min, or when `NewConnectionCount / ActiveConnectionCount` ratio exceeds 0.3 (indicates poor reuse); track HTTP/2 adoption at LB and alert if it drops below 80%; monitor TLS handshake latency p95 > 20ms.

bottlenecks.title: Slow/flapping health checks cause traffic blackholing or oscillation
bottlenecks.trigger: The configured policy is `/healthz` every 5s, eject after 3 consecutive 5xx in 10s. During a partial degradation (e.g., Redis cold start causing web tier to return 5xx on cache-miss paths), all 4–6 web replicas can fail health checks near-simultaneously and get ejected, leaving zero healthy targets. Conversely, a shallow `/healthz` that only checks the process — not Redis/DB connectivity — keeps sick replicas in rotation.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB returns 503 `no healthy upstreams` to all users for 10–30s while replicas bounce back in; or the opposite: backend error rate stays at 5–10% because unhealthy replicas are never evicted; `HealthyHostCount` oscillates sawtooth in dashboards.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement a layered `/healthz` with separate liveness (process up) and readiness (can reach Redis + DB replica) endpoints; use readiness for LB rotation and liveness for orchestrator restarts; add minimum-healthy-target floor (e.g., never eject below 50% of pool — ALB `minimum_healthy_targets.count`); add health-check jitter and use `unhealthy_threshold=3, healthy_threshold=2, interval=5s` with 2s timeout; gate ejection on connection-failure vs 5xx to avoid app-bug-induced total outage.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when `HealthyHostCount` drops below 50% of `TargetGroup` size for > 30s; alert on health-check flap rate (state transitions per minute) > 2; track `HTTPCode_ELB_503_Count` and page if > 0.1% of requests over 1 min; dashboard per-target health-check latency p95 > 500ms.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Load Balancer is here For an app serving 5M daily users with a 99.95% availability target (only 22 minutes of downtime per month), you cannot point users directly at a single web server. You need *many* stateless web replicas so traffic can be spread out and any one of them can die without taking the site down. But clients only know one hostname — `api.example.com` — so *something* has to sit behind that hostname, accept every incoming connection, and fan it out across the healthy replica pool. That something is the L7 load balancer. It's also the natural place to terminate TLS once (instead of on every replica) and to run health checks that eject sick replicas in seconds. ## What happens without it If clients hit a single web server directly, that server is both your throughput ceiling and your single point of failure — one crash and every user in the region sees connection refused. Even if you ran multiple web servers and used DNS round-robin instead, a dead server's IP would keep receiving traffic for minutes (resolvers ignore TTLs) while the operator scrambles to edit DNS records. The web tier can't autoscale meaningfully either, because new replicas have no front door. ## The numbers Peak read traffic is ~5K QPS, and each web replica handles ~10ms per request, so one replica sustains only ~100 concurrent in-flight requests. You need 4–6 replicas minimum — and the LB is what turns those 4–6 boxes into one addressable service, picking the least-loaded healthy target per request. ## Trade-off The LB becomes the regional doorway: if it's misconfigured or its TLS cert expires, the whole region goes dark even though every backend is healthy.

web.name: Web Tier (Stateless App Servers)
web.summary: Stateless Node/Go/Java servers rendering dynamic pages and API responses.

sections.heading: Statelessness
sections.body: No session state in memory. User session lives in a signed cookie or Redis keyed by session id. Any replica can serve any request → trivially horizontally scalable.

sections.heading: Read path
sections.body:
1. `GET /api/profile/:id`
2. Try `redis.GET profile:{id}` — 95% hit rate target
3. On miss: `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id =:id` from read replica
4. Backfill Redis with TTL 10m, return response

sections.heading: Write path
sections.body:
1. `POST /api/profile/:id` with new fields
2. `UPDATE users SET... WHERE id =:id` on primary
3. `DEL profile:{id}` in Redis (invalidate — don't write-through to avoid race)
4. Return 200; replicas catch up asynchronously (typically <100ms lag)

sections.heading: Scaling
sections.body: Peak 5K read QPS, ~10ms service time → ~50 concurrent in-flight requests. 4–6 replicas at moderate utilization, plus headroom for traffic spikes. Autoscale on CPU at 60%.

gained: No capacity planning at low traffic
lost: Cold starts add 50–300ms on p99
DB/Redis connection churn hurts tail latency
Per-request cost passes EC2 around 5K sustained QPS

gained: Simplest possible deploy; no LB, no discovery
lost: Single point of failure — any crash = downtime
Vertical scaling ceiling hits quickly (usually before 10K QPS)

bottlenecks.title: Connection pool exhaustion to DB primary during cache outage
bottlenecks.trigger: Redis cluster failover or cold-start after deploy. With 95% cache hit rate, only ~250 QPS hit the DB normally; on full cache miss, all 5K peak read QPS + 500 write QPS fall through. At ~10ms DB service time, this needs ~55 concurrent DB connections across 4–6 web replicas — but typical pool size is 10–20 per replica (60–120 total), and reads now target the primary (not replicas) because of the read-your-writes routing rule, concentrating load.
bottlenecks.symptom: Web tier request latency jumps from ~10ms to hundreds of ms or seconds; `pg_stat_activity` shows connection pool saturation; web replicas return 503 `pool timeout` errors; LB health checks may fail, cascading into replica ejection and total regional outage.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode between web tier and DB (handles 1000s of client conns → 50 server conns); size application pool at ~20 conns/replica with 500ms acquire timeout; implement request-coalescing (singleflight pattern) so N concurrent misses on the same key fire one DB query; keep the read-your-writes window short (1s) and narrow (per-user, not global) so cache-miss reads still prefer replicas.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when `pg_stat_activity.count` > 70% of `max_connections` for 30s; track pool-acquire-wait-time p95 at the web tier and alert if > 50ms; monitor cache-hit ratio and page if it drops below 90% for 2 min (predicts the fallthrough storm before pool saturates).

bottlenecks.title: Concurrency cap (3000) saturates under retry storms and slow downstreams
bottlenecks.trigger: The web tier's 3000-concurrency cap is sized for 5K QPS × ~10ms = ~50 in-flight requests. But a Redis hiccup pushing service time to 200ms, combined with the documented 3–5x client retry amplification (15–25K QPS), produces 15000 × 0.2s = 3000 in-flight — exactly at the cap. Any further slowdown (slow Redis, replica lag, a hung 3rd-party call in a synchronous handler) immediately blocks new requests.
bottlenecks.symptom: LB reports `HTTPCode_Target_5XX` spikes and `RequestCount` plateaus while `TargetResponseTime` climbs; new requests queue at the LB or get rejected; autoscaling based on CPU (60% threshold) fails to trigger because threads are blocked on I/O, not burning CPU; incident recovers slowly even after the root cause clears.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Autoscale on in-flight-request-count (or LB `ActiveConnectionCount` per target) not CPU; enforce per-downstream timeouts (Redis 50ms, DB 200ms, 3rd-party 500ms) and bulkhead with separate connection pools so a slow dependency can't consume all 3000 slots; implement load-shedding at the handler (reject with 503 + Retry-After when in-flight > 80% of cap) to fail fast instead of queueing; ensure all outbound calls are on async I/O so a blocked handler doesn't pin a thread.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when in-flight requests per replica > 2400 (80% of 3000) for 30s; track per-downstream latency p99 and alert on 2x baseline; dashboard ratio of `ActiveConnectionCount` / `HealthyHostCount` and page if it grows faster than QPS (indicates queueing).

bottlenecks.title: Read-your-writes routing logic breaks under replica lag spikes
bottlenecks.trigger: The write path DELs the Redis key and relies on a ~1s per-user window to route subsequent reads to the primary; replicas typically lag <100ms but can spike to seconds under write bursts (e.g., a bulk import, a schema migration, or the 500 peak write QPS coinciding with a replica restart). If the window is too short, users see their own writes disappear on the next GET; if the window is too long or leaks globally, primary read load multiplies.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users report 'I saved it but it didn't stick' immediately after a POST; support tickets correlate with replication-lag alerts; alternatively, DB primary CPU climbs and write latency degrades because too many reads are being routed to it.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Store the per-user write timestamp in the session store with 2s TTL and route reads to primary only when `now - last_write_ts < max(2s, current_replica_lag + 500ms)`; expose replica lag via `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn` and feed it into the routing decision; on lag > 2s, temporarily route all reads for affected users to primary and alert; use logical replication slots with monitoring to prevent silent lag buildup.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `pg_stat_replication.replay_lag` > 1s for 60s or > 5s instantaneous; track a synthetic write-then-read test from the web tier every 30s and alert on stale reads; monitor ratio of read QPS hitting primary vs replicas and alert if primary reads exceed 10% of total (indicates window-leak bug).

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a stateless web tier is here for *this* problem The design has to serve 5M daily users from multiple regions with 99.95% availability — that's a downtime budget of 22 minutes per month. No single server can handle that, and more importantly, no single server can *fail* without violating the availability target. So the web tier is deliberately designed to be a **herd of identical, interchangeable replicas**: no replica remembers anything about any user between requests. Session data lives in the shared session store, cached reads live in Redis, durable state lives in the SQL tier. A web replica is just a CPU that turns HTTP requests into cache/DB calls and back. ## What happens without statelessness Imagine sessions lived in each web server's RAM. The load balancer would have to pin every user to "their" server (sticky sessions). When that server crashes — or gets terminated during a deploy — every pinned user is logged out mid-action. Autoscaling breaks too: a new replica spun up during a traffic spike has no sessions, so the LB can't send it any sticky traffic, and it sits idle while the hot replicas melt. Operators see uneven CPU across the fleet and angry users reporting random logouts. ## The numbers Peak read traffic is **5K QPS** with ~10ms service time, so roughly 50 requests are in flight at any instant. Spread across 4–6 replicas that's ~10 concurrent requests each — comfortable headroom. If one replica dies, the remaining 3–5 absorb the load instantly because *any* of them can serve *any* user. ## Trade-off Every request now pays a network hop to Redis or the session store to fetch state that used to sit in local memory — you trade a few milliseconds of latency for the ability to lose, replace, or multiply replicas at will.

cache.name: Redis Cache
cache.summary: In-memory KV cache fronting the DB, holding the hot working set.

sections.heading: What's cached
sections.body: Read-through cache keyed by DB row: `profile:{id}`, `post:{id}`, `session:{token}`. TTL 5–10 minutes. The 80/20 rule means ~20% of keys serve ~80% of reads.

sections.heading: Invalidation on write
sections.body: Writes `DEL` the key after the DB UPDATE commits. The next reader takes a miss and refills from the primary (not a replica, to avoid reading stale lagging data). Alternative is write-through, but that adds a race window if DB commit fails after cache write.

sections.heading: Topology
sections.body: 3-node Redis cluster with replication. Sentinel or managed Elasticache handles failover in 5–30s. `allkeys-lru` eviction at 80% maxmemory.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Full cache outage → web tier falls through to DB, which now takes 10x the read QPS. Primary is fine; replicas sweat. p95 degrades from ~5ms to ~20ms but the site stays up.
- Cold start after deploy → first few minutes see elevated DB load until warmed.

lost: No persistence, no replication
No data structures (no sorted sets, streams, pub/sub)
N replicas = N partial caches → lower hit ratio
Invalidation across replicas needs pub/sub anyway

bottlenecks.title: Cold-cache thundering herd after failover or deploy slams the DB primary
bottlenecks.trigger: Redis cluster failover (5–30s Sentinel window), a full cluster restart after maintenance, or a cold deploy wipes the ~2GB hot working set. The normal 95% hit ratio collapses to 0%, so all 5K peak read QPS + 500 write QPS fall through to the SQL tier. Worse: because of the 1s read-your-writes window routing post-write reads to the primary, a burst of writes during recovery concentrates fallthrough reads on the primary instead of spreading across replicas.
bottlenecks.symptom: Immediately after a Redis blip, web-tier p95 latency jumps from ~10ms to hundreds of ms; DB replica CPU spikes to 80–100%; primary connection-pool saturates (web tier has ~60–120 total pool slots vs ~5500 QPS fallthrough); web replicas hit their 3000-concurrency cap and LB starts returning 503s. Site degrades even though Redis itself is 'back up'.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable Redis persistence (AOF every 1s + RDB snapshots) so a restarted node warms from disk instead of empty; use request coalescing / singleflight in the web tier so N concurrent misses on the same key fire one DB query; deploy a 3-node replicated cluster (already specified) with managed Elasticache automatic failover to keep the window under 10s; on planned restarts, pre-warm by replaying a sampled key list from logs before taking traffic; add a short negative-cache TTL (1–2s) on miss to bound stampede duration.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when Redis hit ratio drops below 90% for >60s (normal ~95%); alert when `redis_connected_clients` or `instantaneous_ops_per_sec` drops >50% in 30s; track DB primary + replica QPS and page if either exceeds 2x baseline; synthetic cache-check probe every 10s.

bottlenecks.title: Hot-key / celebrity-key concentration on a single Redis shard
bottlenecks.trigger: The 80/20 rule baked into the design means ~20% of keys serve ~80% of reads — but within that, a viral profile or trending post can concentrate thousands of QPS on a single key. In a 3-node cluster, one key lives on exactly one shard; if `profile:celebrity` receives 2K of the 5K peak read QPS, that shard handles 40%+ of total cluster load while the other two sit at <30%. Redis is single-threaded per shard, so one CPU core becomes the ceiling.
bottlenecks.symptom: Per-shard CPU imbalance visible in Elasticache dashboards — one node at 90%+ while peers are at 20–30%; p99 Redis GET latency on the hot shard drifts from ~1ms to 5–15ms even though average hit ratio looks fine; web-tier p95 increases for a specific subset of endpoints; occasional `CLUSTERDOWN`-style slow commands on the hot shard during rebalance attempts.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Detect hot keys via `redis-cli --hotkeys` or MONITOR sampling; shard hot keys by appending a random suffix (`profile:42:{0..9}`) and fan out reads; add a small in-process LRU (local cache) on each web replica with a 1–5s TTL for detected hot keys — this collapses thousands of reads into per-replica cache hits; for predictable hot objects (homepage feeds), use Redis read replicas per shard and route reads with `READONLY`.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on per-shard CPU variance >30% across the 3-node cluster; run periodic `--hotkeys` scans and alert if any single key exceeds 1K QPS; track per-key latency histograms via Redis slowlog (>5ms threshold); dashboard per-shard `instantaneous_ops_per_sec` and page on >2x median.

bottlenecks.title: Memory pressure triggers premature LRU eviction and hit-ratio collapse
bottlenecks.trigger: The design sizes the hot working set at ~2GB (5M × 20% × 2KB) comfortably in a single Redis node. But growth drivers — user growth to 10M DAU, per-user state creep beyond 2KB, session tokens also sharing the cluster, or large values like cached feed JSON — silently push memory past the 80% `maxmemory` threshold. `allkeys-lru` then evicts aggressively, dropping hit ratio from 95% toward 70–80%.
bottlenecks.symptom: `used_memory` climbs slowly week-over-week; `evicted_keys` counter ticks up from ~0/s to hundreds/s; cache hit ratio trends down with no deploy change; DB replica QPS creeps up proportionally (every 1% hit-ratio drop → +50 QPS to replicas at 5K peak); web-tier p95 drifts from ~10ms toward ~20ms as more requests fall through; on-call notices DB replica CPU rising but can't tie it to any feature release.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Monitor `used_memory / maxmemory` ratio and alert at 70% so headroom exists before evictions start; separate session store from read-cache (they have different sizes and TTLs — sessions ~100 bytes, cached rows ~2KB); enforce per-value size limits (reject caching of values >16KB); shorten TTLs on low-value keys; scale vertically (larger node) or horizontally (more shards) before hit ratio degrades — Elasticache online resharding takes minutes; use `MEMORY USAGE key` sampling to find bloated entries.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when `used_memory_rss / maxmemory > 0.75`; alert on `evicted_keys` rate > 10/s sustained for 5 min; weekly report on average value size by key prefix; alert when rolling 1-hour hit ratio drops below 92% (2pp below the 95% target); track `keyspace_misses / (hits+misses)` as an SLI.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why Redis is here for *this* problem The design is **read-heavy with a 10:1 read/write ratio** and has a **p95 latency budget of 200ms globally**. At 5M DAU generating ~1,160 read QPS average and 5K QPS at peak, serving every read from the SQL primary means the database becomes the bottleneck long before the web tier does — even a well-tuned Postgres handles maybe a few thousand simple SELECTs per second per core, and you'd be burning that capacity re-fetching the same popular profiles over and over. Redis exists to absorb that repeated read traffic in memory, a few milliseconds per lookup, so the SQL tier only sees the reads that actually need fresh data. ## What happens without it Without Redis, every profile view hits a DB replica. The operator sees replica CPU climbing toward 100% during traffic peaks, replication lag creeping up (because replicas are busy serving reads instead of applying writes from the primary), and p95 latency drifting from ~10ms into the tens or hundreds of ms. Users notice the site feels sluggish during peak hours. You'd be forced to add read replicas much earlier — each one costing real money and adding replication fan-out complexity — just to serve traffic that is 80% repeated lookups of the same hot rows. ## The numbers The hot working set is **5M users × 20% × 2KB ≈ 2GB** — trivially fits in a single Redis node's RAM. At a 95% hit ratio, only ~250 of the 5K peak read QPS fall through to the DB; without cache, all 5,000 hit the replicas — a **20× load multiplier**. ## Trade-off You accept a cache-invalidation problem on writes (DEL the key, next reader re-warms from primary) in exchange for an order-of-magnitude reduction in DB load.

dbprimary.name: DB Primary / Master (SQL)
dbprimary.summary: Single master Postgres/MySQL node owning all writes and acting as replication source for the slaves, per the chapter's master/slave replication model.

sections.heading: Why SQL at this scale
sections.body: 500 write QPS peak is comfortably within a well-tuned single primary (typical Postgres on NVMe handles 5–10K write TPS). Transactions, joins, and mature tooling are worth it until you're forced to shard.

sections.heading: Data model
Replication
sections.body: Asynchronous streaming replication to N read replicas. Lag is typically <100ms; alert at >2s. Writes go here, reads go to replicas (see below).

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Primary dies → a replica is promoted (manual or by a failover agent like Patroni). RTO ~30–60s; any writes not yet replicated are lost.
- Long-running migration can block writes; use tools like pg_repack / gh-ost for online schema changes.

lost: Vendor lock-in to AWS
2–3x the $/hour of vanilla RDS

gained: Horizontally scalable writes without application sharding
lost: Higher per-query latency than a single-node primary
Less mature ecosystem / tooling

bottlenecks.title: Primary is a single point of failure with data-loss window on promotion
bottlenecks.trigger: Primary node hardware failure, AZ outage, or a runaway query OOMing the process. With async streaming replication, any writes committed on the primary but not yet shipped to the promoted replica (~50–200ms of WAL, up to several seconds under load) are lost on failover. RTO is 30–60s with Patroni — well beyond the 22-min/month availability budget if it happens twice.
bottlenecks.symptom: All writes (500 peak QPS) fail with connection refused or timeout for 30–60s; web-tier 5xx spikes on every POST; after promotion, some users report 'I saved it but it's gone' because their commit was in un-replicated WAL; read-your-writes routing window points at a now-dead primary IP.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use Patroni + etcd (or managed Aurora with ~10s replica promotion) for automated failover; enable synchronous replication to at least one replica (`synchronous_commit=on`, `synchronous_standby_names='FIRST 1 (replica1,replica2)'`) to bound data loss to zero at a ~1–3ms write-latency cost; keep a VIP or DNS alias (`db-primary.internal`) that Patroni flips so the web tier reconnects automatically; run quarterly failover drills.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `pg_is_in_recovery` state changes; monitor `pg_stat_replication.write_lag` and `flush_lag` and page if sync replica lag exceeds 500ms; external synthetic write probe every 10s alerting on >3 consecutive failures; track Patroni leader-election events.

bottlenecks.title: Write amplification on cache-miss storms saturates primary connections
bottlenecks.trigger: Redis failover or cold start (per the cache component's documented bottleneck) collapses the 95% hit ratio, and the read-your-writes routing rule concentrates post-write reads on the primary. Normal write load is 500 peak QPS against a ~400-concurrency cap, but a cache blip adds thousands of primary reads on top. `max_connections` is typically 100–200; with 4–6 web replicas × 10–20 pool slots = 60–120 client conns, leaving no headroom for reads + writes + replication slots.
bottlenecks.symptom: `pg_stat_activity` hits `max_connections`; new web-tier queries fail with `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved`; write latency jumps from ~10ms to seconds as locks queue; replication slots may stall, causing replica lag to climb past the 2s alert threshold; the write path's UPDATE + DEL sequence slows, widening the stale-read window.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode in front of the primary (collapses 1000s of client conns → 50 server conns); set `max_connections=200`, `pgbouncer pool_size=40`, `reserve_pool_size=5`; enforce `statement_timeout=2s` and `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout=10s`; route reads strictly to replicas except within a narrow per-user 1s read-your-writes window stored in the session (not a global toggle); add request coalescing in the web tier so N concurrent misses on the same key fire one SQL query.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when `pg_stat_activity` count > 70% of `max_connections` for 30s; alert on PgBouncer `cl_waiting > 0` sustained; track percentage of reads hitting primary vs replicas and page if primary reads exceed 10% of total read QPS (indicates read-your-writes window leak).

bottlenecks.title: Long-running migrations / vacuum block writes and burn the availability budget
bottlenecks.trigger: Schema changes on the `users` table (ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN with default, CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY, ALTER TYPE) take AccessExclusiveLock and block all 500 peak QPS of writes plus any reads routed to primary. At 5M users × 2KB ≈ 10GB table, a naive ALTER can hold the lock for tens of minutes. Similarly, autovacuum falling behind on a write-heavy table leads to bloat and eventual wraparound-prevention vacuums that run for hours.
bottlenecks.symptom: Writes stall with `LOG: process still waiting for AccessExclusiveLock`; web-tier request queue fills; POST endpoints time out; p95 write latency goes from ~10ms to tens of seconds; the 22-min monthly downtime budget is spent in a single deploy; worst case, transaction ID wraparound forces an emergency read-only mode.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Mandate online schema-change tooling: `pg_repack` for table rewrites, `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, `ALTER TABLE... ADD COLUMN... NULL` (no default) followed by a backfill in batches; use `gh-ost`/`pt-online-schema-change` on MySQL; set `lock_timeout=2s` on migration sessions so a blocked ALTER fails fast instead of queueing writes; tune autovacuum aggressively for `users` (`autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor=0.05`, `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit=2000`); monitor `age(datfrozenxid)`.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on any `pg_locks` entry with `granted=false` waiting > 5s; alert when `age(datfrozenxid) > 500M` (well before the 2B wraparound hard stop); track `pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup / n_live_tup` on `users` and alert at > 20%; pre-deploy gate that rejects migrations containing bare `ALTER TABLE` or `CREATE INDEX` without `CONCURRENTLY`.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the DB Primary is here For a read-heavy app serving 5M daily users, you need one authoritative place where writes land and conflicts get resolved. The primary is that place. Redis is fast but volatile (a cluster restart wipes the hot set), read replicas are eventually consistent (they lag the primary by ~100ms), and the session store holds ephemeral tokens — none of them are the source of truth. When Ada edits her bio, that UPDATE has to commit *somewhere* with durable guarantees (WAL fsync, unique constraints, transactions) so that a crashed replica or a cold cache can always be rebuilt from it. The primary is the root of the whole data tier: replicas stream from it, caches fill from it, workers read authoritative state from it. ## What happens without it If writes were spread across replicas directly, two users grabbing the same email address could both succeed on different nodes — and replication would later crash trying to reconcile them. The operator would see replication slots diverging, unique-constraint violations in the logs, and manual data-repair tickets piling up. Users would see duplicate accounts or "saved" changes that silently vanish when a different replica won a conflict. ## The numbers Peak write load is **500 QPS** (10:1 read:write ratio against 5K peak reads). A well-tuned Postgres primary on NVMe handles 5–10K write TPS, so one node has **10–20× headroom** — meaning you don't need sharding yet, and the design gets transactions and joins for free until ~50M DAU. ## Trade-off You accept a single-writer bottleneck (and a 30–60s failover window) in exchange for strong consistency and simple application code.

dbreplica.name: DB Read Replica (Slave)
dbreplica.summary: Read-only slave streaming from the master; serves the read tier and analytics.

sections.heading: Role
sections.body: In the book's master/slave terminology, slaves take the bulk of SELECT traffic. The web tier uses a read/write split at the connection-pool level: writes → master, reads → slaves via a replica-aware driver. Book's Figure 1-5 motivates the split with two advantages: better performance (reads fan out) and reliability/HA (data survives a single node loss).

sections.heading: Replication lag
sections.body: Async streaming — typically <100ms. After a write, the same user might briefly read stale data from a replica. Solution: route the user's next read to primary for ~1s after a write, or accept eventual consistency.

sections.heading: Scaling
sections.body: Add replicas horizontally to handle more reads. Past ~5–10 replicas, replication fan-out becomes a bottleneck — consider cascading replicas or moving to a clustered DB. Beyond that, the book's next step is horizontal sharding (partition by user_id % N, see 'Database sharding' section of the chapter).

sections.heading: Failover behaviour (per book)
sections.body: If a slave dies, reads temporarily route to the master while a replacement slave is spun up and rebuilt from a base backup. If the master dies, a slave is promoted to master; the chapter notes promoted-slave lag means recovery scripts may be needed to replay missing writes.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Replica crashes → LB-style health check removes it from the pool; reads rebalance.
- Replication breaks (slot fills, WAL overflow) → replica falls further behind; must be rebuilt from a base backup.

lost: Transaction-level pooling breaks some session features
Operational extra hop

gained: Write throughput scales linearly with shard count
Each shard holds a bounded slice of data
lost: Cross-shard joins become a denormalization problem
Resharding is operationally expensive — book explicitly points to consistent hashing (Ch. 5) as the mitigation
Hot-key/celebrity shards need further partitioning

bottlenecks.title: Replication lag spike under write bursts starves read-your-writes correctness
bottlenecks.trigger: Streaming replication is async; at peak 500 write QPS plus bulk operations (imports, backfills, schema migrations), replicas can fall from the normal <100ms lag to seconds or tens of seconds. Compounded by Redis cache-miss storms routing ~4,750 of the 5K peak read QPS to replicas, a replica under both heavy read and replay load falls further behind because WAL replay is single-threaded in Postgres/MySQL.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users report 'I saved it but it didn't show up' immediately after a write; the web tier's 1s read-your-writes window is insufficient, so reads routed to replicas return pre-UPDATE rows; support tickets correlate with `pg_stat_replication.replay_lag` alerts; dashboards show replay_lag climbing sawtooth during write peaks.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Monitor `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn` lag and feed it into the web tier's routing decision — when lag > 1s, extend the read-your-writes window or temporarily route affected users to the primary; use Postgres 14+ parallel apply or logical replication with multiple workers; isolate bulk operations (imports, analytics) to a dedicated replica so user-facing replicas stay fresh; cap write bursts via rate-limiting at the web tier.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `pg_stat_replication.replay_lag > 1s` for 60s or > 5s instantaneous; synthetic write-then-read probe every 30s from the web tier with alert on stale reads; dashboard per-replica lag distribution (p50/p95/p99) and page if p95 exceeds 500ms.

bottlenecks.title: Cache-miss storm concentrates ~5K QPS on replicas, saturating CPU and connection pools
bottlenecks.trigger: Redis failover or cold start (5–30s Sentinel window) collapses the 95% cache hit ratio. Reads that normally hit the cache — ~4,750 of the 5K peak read QPS — fall through to replicas. With the concurrency cap at ~500 per replica and typical `max_connections` of 100–200, a 2-replica pool receives ~2,500 QPS each, overwhelming CPU (replicas are also busy applying WAL) and connection slots.
bottlenecks.symptom: Replica CPU pins at 100% during Redis blips; `pg_stat_activity` approaches `max_connections` on each replica; query latency p95 jumps from ~5ms to hundreds of ms; some queries fail with `FATAL: remaining connection slots are reserved`; replay_lag climbs because WAL apply competes with query load; web-tier 3000-concurrency cap saturates cascading into 503s.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy PgBouncer in transaction-pooling mode in front of each replica (collapses 1000s of client conns → ~40 server conns); run at least 3 replicas with LB-style health-checked routing so load divides; implement request coalescing (singleflight) in the web tier so N concurrent misses on the same key fire one SQL query; pre-provision replica capacity at 40% utilization so headroom absorbs a 10x cache-miss multiplier; set `statement_timeout=2s` to shed load fast.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when any replica's `pg_stat_activity` count > 70% of `max_connections` for 30s; alert on replica CPU > 75% for 2 min; track cache hit ratio and page when it drops below 90% (predicts the replica storm before it lands); dashboard per-replica QPS and alert on >2x baseline.

bottlenecks.title: Replication slot overflow or WAL disk exhaustion silently breaks a replica
bottlenecks.trigger: A replica disconnects (network blip, long GC pause, maintenance) while its replication slot on the primary retains WAL to guarantee resumability. At 500 peak write QPS generating meaningful WAL volume (several GB/hour on a write-heavy `users` table), a disconnection of more than a few hours can fill the primary's WAL disk — or the replica falls so far behind that catching up takes longer than the retention, forcing a full rebuild from base backup (tens of minutes to hours for a 10GB+ table).
bottlenecks.symptom: Primary's `pg_wal` directory grows unboundedly and eventually fills the disk, threatening to crash the primary (affecting ALL writes, not just the broken replica); alternatively, the replica falls indefinitely behind and the on-call engineer must rebuild it from a base backup, during which read capacity is reduced and surviving replicas run hotter; `pg_replication_slots.active = false` with growing `restart_lsn` gap.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set `max_slot_wal_keep_size` (Postgres 13+) to a bounded value (e.g., 100GB) so a dead slot gets invalidated instead of filling the primary's disk — accept that the replica needs rebuild rather than risk the primary; automate replica rebuild via `pg_basebackup` + WAL streaming; monitor slot lag and proactively drop slots for replicas offline >1h; keep 2+ replicas so losing one to rebuild doesn't halve read capacity.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `pg_replication_slots.active = false` for >5 min; alert when `pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn, restart_lsn)` exceeds 10GB on any slot; page when primary `pg_wal` disk usage >70%; alert on `pg_stat_replication` missing an expected replica entry for >2 min.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the read replica is here This app is **read-heavy at a 10:1 ratio**: 5,000 peak read QPS versus only 500 write QPS. If every SELECT went to the primary, the primary would be doing two jobs at once — accepting writes *and* answering a flood of reads — and it's the same box that has to durably commit every write with fsync. Reads would starve writes, and writes would slow reads. The read replica exists so the primary can focus on being the authoritative writer while a pool of streaming-replicated copies soaks up the SELECT traffic. It's also a free HA bonus: if the primary dies, a replica gets promoted instead of the site going read-only. ## What happens without it Operator-side: primary CPU pins at 90%+ during peak hours, write latency climbs from ~10ms into the hundreds, and replication-lag-style problems are replaced with far worse lock-contention problems on the primary itself. User-side: saves feel sluggish and occasionally time out, especially when a Redis cache blip sends a storm of reads at the DB. The cache tier and web tier both take the hit — web replicas queue up waiting on slow DB responses and eventually saturate their 3000-concurrency cap, cascading into 503s. ## The numbers At a 95% Redis hit ratio, only ~250 of the 5,000 peak read QPS fall through to SQL. But on a cache cold-start, all 5,000 hit the DB. Split across 3 replicas that's ~1,660 QPS each — tolerable. Sent to a lone primary already handling 500 writes/s, it's a meltdown. ## Trade-off You accept ~100ms of replication lag, meaning a user can briefly read stale data right after their own write.

session.name: Session / NoSQL Store
session.summary: Shared out-of-tier session and profile store that lets the web tier be stateless — the pivot point of the chapter's stateless-web-tier design.

sections.heading: Why this exists (per book)
sections.body: Chapter 1's 'Stateless web tier' section (Figures 1-12 to 1-14) removes session state from web servers so any request can be served by any server. The book specifically picks a NoSQL data store here because it is easy to scale horizontally, though Memcached/Redis or a relational DB would also work.

sections.heading: What's stored
sections.body:
- Session tokens → `{user_id, expires_at, csrf}`
- Lightweight per-user state (feature flags, UI preferences)
- Anything that would otherwise sit in in-process memory on a web server

sections.heading: Consequences of statelessness
sections.body:
- No sticky sessions needed at the LB → load spreads evenly
- Web tier can autoscale on CPU with no session migration problem
- Rolling deploys don't log users out

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Session store outage → users cannot authenticate on new requests; existing signed JWTs (if used) keep working. Mitigation: short-TTL JWT as a fallback identity layer.
- Cross-DC replication lag can make a session look expired on the other coast for a few seconds after creation.

lost: Revocation is hard (tokens valid until expiry)
Token size inflates every request

gained: Same tech as the cache tier — one fewer thing to operate
lost: In-memory → session loss on full cluster failure
Cross-region replication is extra config

bottlenecks.title: Session store outage locks out the entire logged-in user base
bottlenecks.trigger: The session store is on the synchronous auth path for every request from the web tier — at 5K peak read QPS + 500 write QPS, every one of those requests does a session lookup before business logic. A NoSQL cluster failure, failover window, or network partition between web tier and session store means authentication fails for all 5M DAU simultaneously, even though DB, cache, and web tier are healthy.
bottlenecks.symptom: Sudden global spike in 401/403 responses while backend dashboards (DB, Redis, web-tier CPU) look green; users report being logged out mid-session and unable to log back in; LB health checks pass but user-facing error rate jumps to 100% on authenticated endpoints; the 22-min/month availability budget burns in a single incident.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy a multi-AZ replicated NoSQL cluster (DynamoDB global tables, Cassandra with RF=3, or managed MongoDB with replica set) with automatic failover <10s; add a short-lived signed JWT as a fallback identity layer so existing sessions survive a session-store blip (JWT validates cryptographically, no lookup needed); set aggressive client timeout (200ms) with one retry to a secondary replica; circuit-break to JWT-only mode when session-store error rate > 5%.
bottlenecks.detection: Synthetic login probe every 10s alerting on 2 consecutive failures; alert when session-store p99 latency exceeds 50ms or error rate exceeds 0.5% over 1 min; dashboard ratio of authenticated-request-failures / total-authenticated-requests and page when > 1%; monitor replica lag and failover events.

bottlenecks.title: Cross-region replication lag breaks sessions on geo-DNS failover
bottlenecks.trigger: Geo-DNS routes users to the nearest region (~60/40 US-East/US-West split). A session created in US-East must replicate to US-West before that user can be served from US-West — either on failover or when they travel. NoSQL cross-region replication typically runs 100ms–several seconds; during DC outage failover, 40% of users (~2M DAU) suddenly hit the survivor region where their just-created session may not exist yet.
bottlenecks.symptom: After a region failover or for users whose geo-routing flips (mobile roaming, ISP changes), login appears successful but the very next request returns 401 'session not found'; users report being randomly logged out; support tickets cluster around failover windows; session-creation QPS in one region doesn't match session-read QPS in the peer region.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a session store with multi-region active-active replication and bounded staleness (DynamoDB Global Tables, Cosmos DB, or Cassandra multi-DC with LOCAL_QUORUM writes + eventual cross-DC); on session miss, fall back to reading from the origin region synchronously for a 5s grace window after session creation; embed session creation timestamp in the cookie and skip strict validation for sessions <10s old; use short-TTL JWTs as a portable fallback identity layer that does not require replication.
bottlenecks.detection: Track cross-region replication lag as an SLI and alert on p95 > 2s; synthetic probe that creates a session in region A and reads it from region B within 1s, alerting on > 0.5% miss rate; dashboard session-not-found rate per region and correlate with geo-DNS flips; measure session-age distribution of 401 responses (spike at <10s indicates replication lag).

bottlenecks.title: Per-request session lookup adds a mandatory network hop to every authenticated call
bottlenecks.trigger: Making the web tier stateless means every one of 5K peak read QPS + 500 write QPS pays a network round-trip to the session store (sim shows 3–10ms service time). Under normal operation this is 3–10ms of the 200ms p95 budget; under session-store degradation (GC pause, hot partition, cross-AZ slowdown) this balloons to 50–200ms and consumes the entire budget before the handler has done any real work.
bottlenecks.symptom: Web-tier p95 latency correlates 1:1 with session-store latency; even on trivial endpoints (hot cache hits that should be ~10ms end-to-end), p95 drifts to 20–30ms when session store has a bad minute; web-tier 3000-concurrency cap fills because handlers block on session reads; DB and Redis dashboards look fine but users report site feels slow.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add an in-process LRU session cache per web replica (TTL 30s, ~100KB RAM for 1000 active sessions) so repeat requests from the same user in a short window skip the network hop; use signed JWTs for the common case and only hit the session store for revocation checks on sensitive operations; enforce a strict 50ms session-store timeout with circuit breaker to fail fast; collocate session store in the same AZ as the web tier and pin reads with LOCAL_ONE consistency.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when session-store p95 latency > 15ms for 2 min (5x normal); track session-store latency as a separate histogram in web-tier traces and alert when it exceeds 20% of total request latency; monitor in-process session-cache hit ratio and alert if it drops below 70%; dashboard web-tier in-flight-request count vs session-store latency to catch correlation early.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the session store is here for *this* problem The whole design hinges on the web tier being **stateless** — 4–6 interchangeable replicas behind a load balancer, any of which can serve any request. But users still need to stay logged in across requests. If each web server kept session data in its own local memory, the load balancer would have to pin every user to "their" server (sticky sessions), which defeats the point: autoscaling breaks, rolling deploys log everyone out, and a single replica crash boots thousands of users. The session store exists as the **shared out-of-process memory** that lets any replica serve any user — it's the pivot that makes the stateless web tier actually work. ## What happens without it Picture a deploy during peak hours. Replicas get replaced one by one; every user pinned to a replaced server suddenly finds their cart empty, their login gone, their multi-step form reset. The operator sees a flood of re-login traffic hammering the auth path, uneven CPU across the fleet (hot replicas melting while fresh ones sit idle because no sticky traffic routes to them), and angry support tickets. Autoscaling is effectively broken — you can't add capacity where it's needed. ## The numbers At **5M DAU × ~20 page views/day = 100M authenticated requests/day**, peaking at ~5K QPS. Every one of those requests needs to answer "who is this user?" in a few milliseconds. Pinning 5M users to specific replicas is impossible when the fleet is constantly churning; a shared store serving 5K lookups/sec at ~3–10ms each is trivial. ## Trade-off Every authenticated request now pays a mandatory network hop (3–10ms) that used to be a local memory read — you buy replica fungibility with a small, fixed latency tax.

mq.name: Message Queue
mq.summary: Durable buffer that decouples producers (web tier) from consumers (workers); the chapter's answer to 'scale components independently'.

sections.heading: Role (per book)
sections.body: Chapter 1's 'Message queue' section introduces a queue to absorb slow or bursty work (the book's canonical example is photo processing — crop/sharpen/blur). Web servers publish jobs; worker pool consumes. Producer and consumer can be scaled independently: queue depth goes up → add workers; queue depth stays empty → remove workers.

sections.heading: What goes in the queue
sections.body:
- Photo/video processing jobs
- Email / SMS / push notification sends
- Search-index update events
- Webhook fanout to 3rd parties
Anything that can be done asynchronously and whose failure should not fail the user's request.

sections.heading: Durability
sections.body: Messages are persisted (replicated in RabbitMQ / Kafka log-backed) so a crashed consumer does not lose work. Visibility-timeout / ack pattern ensures a message is redelivered if the worker crashes mid-process.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Queue down → web tier can fall back to best-effort in-memory buffering or respond with a 'queued' status; alternatively, circuit-break the async path and degrade.
- Poison messages (fail every retry) should be parked on a dead-letter queue for manual review.

gained: Natural fit for event-sourcing / stream processing
lost: Heavier to operate than RabbitMQ/SQS
At-least-once delivery pushes dedupe into consumers

gained: Fully managed, no brokers to run
lost: Higher per-message latency than a self-hosted broker
No replay / log semantics (standard queues)

bottlenecks.title: Unbounded backlog when workers can't keep up with enqueue rate
bottlenecks.trigger: Design specifies ~200 jobs/s steady-state async volume with worker pool sized for ~2x burst. A downstream dependency outage (3rd-party email API, image-processing service) or a traffic spike (photo upload event, marketing blast) can push enqueue to 500–1000/s while consumer throughput drops toward zero. At 200 net jobs/s accumulating with avg payload ~10KB, backlog grows ~170MB/min — tens of GB within hours, exhausting broker disk or RabbitMQ's memory-high-watermark threshold.
bottlenecks.symptom: Queue depth climbs monotonically on dashboards; consumer lag grows from seconds to hours; in RabbitMQ, publishers get flow-controlled and web-tier POSTs (e.g., photo uploads) slow from ~20ms to seconds as publish blocks; in Kafka, broker disk fills and ISR shrinks; users see delayed emails/notifications; eventually broker OOMs or disk-fulls, taking the async path fully offline.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set per-queue max-length and max-length-bytes limits with overflow policy `reject-publish` so the web tier fails fast instead of drowning the broker; autoscale workers on queue depth / consumer lag (not CPU) with aggressive scale-up (e.g., +50% workers per 1000 backlog); route overflow to a dead-letter queue for later replay; implement priority queues so user-visible jobs (thumbnails) preempt batch jobs (search reindex); circuit-break publishers when backlog exceeds 10x normal depth and degrade gracefully (e.g., skip async thumbnails, return original image).
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when queue depth > 10,000 messages or > 5 minutes of consumer-lag-at-current-rate for 2 min; alert on broker disk > 70% or memory > 60% of high-watermark; track publish-to-ack latency p95 at the web tier and alert on > 50ms (indicates flow control); dashboard enqueue-rate vs dequeue-rate and page when ratio exceeds 1.5 for 5 min.

bottlenecks.title: Poison messages cause infinite redelivery loops that starve healthy traffic
bottlenecks.trigger: The at-least-once delivery + visibility-timeout pattern means a message that crashes the worker (malformed payload, unsupported image format, 4xx from a 3rd-party API that's actually permanent not transient) gets redelivered forever. At ~200 jobs/s, even a 0.1% poison rate produces ~17,000 poisoned messages/day that each consume a worker slot (pool concurrency 200) on every redelivery cycle, displacing real work.
bottlenecks.symptom: Worker error rate creeps up while throughput drops; the same message_id appears repeatedly in worker error logs; queue depth stays flat or grows slowly despite healthy-looking consumer count; specific users report their uploads silently never processing; worker pool CPU looks busy but useful-work-per-second declines; visibility-timeout redeliveries dominate the broker's redelivered-message counter.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Configure a dead-letter queue (DLQ) with max-delivery-count of 3–5 (RabbitMQ `x-dead-letter-exchange` + `x-delivery-limit`; SQS `maxReceiveCount`; Kafka consumer-side with a retry topic + DLQ topic pattern); distinguish transient vs permanent errors in the worker and nack-to-DLQ immediately on permanent errors (4xx, schema violations) rather than waiting for retry exhaustion; emit a metric per DLQ arrival with the failure reason; build a DLQ-replay tool for manual triage after fixing the bug.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on DLQ depth > 100 messages or DLQ arrival rate > 1/s sustained; alert when broker-reported `redelivered` message rate exceeds 5% of total delivery rate; dashboard per-message-type error rate at the worker and alert on any type > 1%; track unique-message-ids processed vs total-deliveries ratio and alert if ratio drops below 0.9.

bottlenecks.title: Broker is a single point of failure on the async path
bottlenecks.trigger: The queue sits between the web tier and the worker pool for every async operation (photo processing, email, webhook fanout, search index updates). A broker cluster failover, network partition, or AZ outage makes publish fail for all ~200 jobs/s of async work; at peak upload events this can be higher. Self-hosted RabbitMQ/Kafka failovers typically take 10–60s; managed SQS is more resilient but cross-region failover is not automatic.
bottlenecks.symptom: Web-tier POSTs that enqueue async work (photo upload, signup → welcome email) fail with 500 or hang on publish timeout; if the web tier blocks on publish, the 3000-concurrency cap fills quickly at 200 jobs/s × publish timeout; users see 'upload failed' errors even though the primary DB write succeeded, producing inconsistent state (row exists, thumbnail never generated); worker pool idles while backlog-of-intent piles up at producers.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Deploy broker as a replicated cluster across 3 AZs (RabbitMQ quorum queues with RF=3, Kafka with min.insync.replicas=2 and RF=3, or managed SQS/MSK); make publish asynchronous with a bounded local outbox in the web tier (transactional outbox pattern: INSERT job row in same DB transaction as the user write, separate relay process publishes to broker) so broker outage doesn't fail user requests; set publish timeout to 500ms with circuit breaker that trips to outbox-only mode; for critical paths, keep a secondary broker or fall back to writing to S3 + a reconciliation worker.
bottlenecks.detection: Synthetic publish+consume probe every 10s alerting on 2 consecutive failures; alert on broker `connected_nodes` < cluster_size or Kafka `under_replicated_partitions > 0`; track web-tier publish latency p99 and alert on > 100ms; monitor outbox table depth as an SLI and alert if relay lag exceeds 30s.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the queue is here for *this* problem This design has a strict **p95 latency budget of 200ms globally**. But some things users trigger — resizing an uploaded photo, sending a welcome email, fanning out a webhook to a third party — take hundreds of milliseconds or even seconds. If the web tier did that work inline, a single photo upload could tie up a web replica for 2 seconds, and the user would stare at a spinner while the third-party email API drags its feet. The queue exists to let the web tier say "I accepted your work, it'll happen" in ~20ms, hand the job off, and move on. Producers (web tier) and consumers (workers) also scale independently — a traffic spike that quintuples uploads doesn't need five times the web servers, just more workers chewing the backlog. ## What happens without it Without the queue, every photo upload blocks a web replica until the resize finishes. Operators see the web tier's 3000-concurrency cap saturate during upload bursts, p95 climb into the seconds, and the LB start returning 503s. Worse, when the email provider has a bad minute, *every* signup fails — a transient downstream problem becomes a user-visible outage. ## The numbers The design estimates **~200 async jobs/s** off the synchronous path. At ~200ms per job that's 40 worker-seconds of work per wall-clock second — work that would otherwise consume ~40 of the web tier's ~50 concurrent slots at peak, leaving almost nothing for actual page rendering. ## Trade-off You accept that async work is "eventually done" (seconds to minutes later) and must be idempotent because messages can be redelivered.

worker.name: Worker Pool
worker.summary: Consumer processes that pull jobs off the queue and run them asynchronously — photo processing, emails, webhook fanout.

sections.heading: Role
