sections.body: The book's photo customization example (Figure 1-18) is the canonical case: user uploads a photo → web tier enqueues resize/sharpen jobs → workers process off the queue. User's request returns immediately after enqueue.

sections.heading: Autoscaling signal
sections.body: Scale on queue depth / consumer lag, not CPU. A backlog means more workers are needed; empty queue means workers can scale down.

sections.heading: Idempotency
sections.body: Workers MUST be idempotent — messages can be redelivered after a crash. Use the job id as a dedupe key (e.g., `INSERT... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` keyed on job_id).

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Worker crashes mid-job → message reappears after visibility timeout, retried by another worker.
- Downstream dependency (e.g., 3rd-party API) down → jobs backlog in queue until recovery; no user-visible error.

lost: Lost on web-server restart
No retry / DLQ / observability
Ties worker lifecycle to request lifecycle

bottlenecks.title: Non-idempotent workers corrupt state under at-least-once redelivery
bottlenecks.trigger: The queue provides at-least-once delivery: a worker that crashes or times out after partial side-effects (DB write committed, 3rd-party API called, email sent) has its message redelivered after visibility-timeout. At ~200 jobs/s with failureRate 0.002, that's ~400 crashes/day where redelivery can re-execute side-effects; any worker handler that isn't keyed on job_id will double-charge, double-email, or double-index.
bottlenecks.symptom: Users receive duplicate welcome emails or push notifications; search index has duplicate entries for the same source row; photo processing produces N copies of the same thumbnail in object storage; 3rd-party webhook consumers complain about replayed events; support tickets cluster around 'I got 3 emails'; DB rows have duplicate child records despite unique-by-intent semantics.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce idempotency by job_id at every side-effect: `INSERT... ON CONFLICT (job_id) DO NOTHING` for DB writes, content-hashed object keys (s3://bucket/thumb/{sha256}.jpg) for image outputs, Idempotency-Key header on all outbound 3rd-party HTTP calls, and a processed-jobs table with TTL-based cleanup as the dedupe backstop. Code-review gate that rejects worker handlers without an idempotency key.
bottlenecks.detection: Track ratio of broker-reported `redelivered=true` messages per worker type; alert if > 1% sustained. Emit a metric on dedupe-hit (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING row count) and alert on spikes. Synthetic test that force-crashes a worker mid-job and asserts no duplicate side-effects.

bottlenecks.title: Slow downstream dependency exhausts worker pool concurrency (200)
bottlenecks.trigger: Worker pool concurrency is capped at 200 with service time 50–300ms (design sim). A 3rd-party dependency (email provider, image-processing API, webhook endpoint) degrading from 200ms to 5s consumes all 200 slots within seconds at the 200 jobs/s enqueue rate (200 slots / 5s = 40 jobs/s drain vs 200/s arrival). All other async work — thumbnails, search-index updates, critical notifications — starves behind the slow dependency.
bottlenecks.symptom: Queue depth climbs monotonically while worker CPU stays low (threads blocked on I/O); unrelated job types (thumbnails) delayed by hours even though their own dependencies are healthy; p95 job-completion latency spikes across the board; autoscaling-on-queue-depth triggers but new workers immediately block on the same slow dependency, wasting capacity.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Bulkhead by job type: separate worker pools (or separate queues) per dependency class so a slow email API can't starve photo processing. Enforce per-call timeouts matched to SLO (email: 2s, webhook: 5s, image API: 10s) with circuit breakers that fast-fail to DLQ after 50% error rate over 30s. Use per-dependency semaphores (e.g., max 50 of 200 slots for email) so one bad dependency is capped. Run workers on async I/O so blocked calls don't pin OS threads.
bottlenecks.detection: Dashboard per-job-type in-flight count and alert when any single type exceeds 60% of pool (120 slots). Alert on per-dependency p95 latency > 2x baseline for 2 min. Track worker slot-utilization vs CPU — alert when utilization > 80% but CPU < 30% (classic blocked-on-I/O signature).

bottlenecks.title: Retry storms on transient failures amplify load into cascading backlog
bottlenecks.trigger: With failureRate 0.002 at 200 jobs/s steady-state, ~400 jobs/s redelivery attempts occur during a 10-minute downstream outage if default visibility timeout is short (e.g., 30s) and retries are unbounded. Combined with the 2x burst headroom designed into the pool, a sustained dependency outage plus synchronized retry attempts pushes effective load to 3–5x normal before DLQ cutoff kicks in.
bottlenecks.symptom: After a brief downstream blip recovers, worker pool stays saturated for 10–30 minutes replaying accumulated retries; queue depth doesn't drain at the expected rate even though enqueue rate returned to normal; the same job_id appears in worker logs 5–10 times; 3rd-party APIs rate-limit the workers as retry traffic exceeds their quota, prolonging the outage.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement exponential backoff with jitter on the consumer side (base 1s, cap 5min, full jitter) by nacking with a delayed-retry queue (RabbitMQ TTL+DLX chain; SQS message-timer; Kafka retry topics with scheduled-delivery). Cap max-delivery-count at 5 and route to DLQ after exhaustion. Distinguish transient (5xx, timeout) from permanent (4xx, schema error) failures — permanents go directly to DLQ without retry. Honor downstream Retry-After headers.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on redelivery rate > 5% of delivery rate sustained for 2 min. Track unique-job-ids-processed / total-deliveries ratio; alert if < 0.85. Dashboard DLQ arrival rate per job type and alert on > 1/s. Monitor per-downstream rate-limit (429) responses and alert on any non-zero rate.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the worker pool is here for *this* problem The design has a hard **p95 latency budget of 200ms globally**, but real apps have work that just can't fit in 200ms: resizing an uploaded photo takes 1–3 seconds, sending a welcome email through a third-party SMTP provider can take 500ms–5s, fanning out a webhook to slow partner APIs is unpredictable. The message queue *accepts* those jobs quickly, but something has to actually *do* them — that's the worker pool. Workers live outside the synchronous request path so the web tier can answer the user in ~20ms ("got it, we're processing your photo") while the heavy lifting happens in the background. ## What happens without it If the web tier did this work inline, a photo upload would pin a web replica for 2+ seconds. The operator would watch the web tier's **3000-concurrency cap** saturate during upload bursts, p95 latency climb into the seconds, and the LB start returning 503s. Worse, when the email provider has a bad minute, *every signup fails* — a transient third-party hiccup becomes a user-visible outage. The DB primary also takes collateral damage because slow requests hold their connections open longer, starving the write pool. ## The numbers The design estimates **~200 async jobs/s** off the synchronous path. At ~200ms average per job, that's 40 worker-seconds of work per wall-clock second — work that would otherwise consume ~40 of the web tier's ~50 concurrent request slots at peak, leaving almost nothing for actual page rendering. ## Trade-off Async work is "eventually done" (seconds to minutes later) and must be idempotent because messages can be redelivered after a worker crash.

operations.title: User request (hot cache hit)
operations.name: User request (hot cache hit)
operations.description: The common case: a dynamic page request whose underlying row is already cached in Redis. p95 ~10ms.

steps.title: Browser requests a profile page
steps.action: User navigates to /profile/42. The browser has a cached DNS answer for api.example.com and reuses a keep-alive TLS connection to the LB.
steps.codeOrCommand:
GET /api/profile/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Cookie: session=abc123
Accept: application/json
steps.note: DNS was resolved via the DNS component on the first navigation; subsequent requests reuse the cached answer for its TTL.

steps.title: LB terminates TLS and picks a web replica
steps.action: The L7 LB terminates TLS, inspects the Host header, and forwards plaintext HTTP to the least-loaded healthy web replica.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# conceptual
upstream = pool.pick(algo="least_conn", healthy_only=True)
forward(req → upstream, protocol=http)

steps.title: Web tier checks Redis first (read-through)
steps.action: The handler extracts `id=42` from the path, authenticates the session cookie, and issues a single Redis GET before touching any DB.

steps.title: Redis returns the row (HIT)
steps.action: In-memory hash lookup, sub-millisecond. Key exists because it was backfilled on a previous miss and has not yet hit its 10m TTL.

steps.title: Web tier serializes and returns the response
steps.action: No DB call needed. Handler wraps the cached JSON in a 200 response with a short Cache-Control for the browser.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return Response( status=200, headers={"Cache-Control": "private, max-age=30", "Content-Type": "application/json"}, body=cached
)

steps.title: LB relays the response
steps.action: Return path of an already-established connection — no fresh routing decision.

steps.title: Browser renders the page
steps.action: Total perceived latency ~10–25ms including network. Most of the budget is spent on the network, not the backend.

operations.title: User request (cache miss — falls through to DB replica)
operations.name: User request (cache miss — falls through to DB replica)
operations.description: Same read, but the key is not in Redis. Web tier reads from a replica, backfills the cache, and returns. p95 ~25ms.

steps.title: Browser requests an unvisited profile
steps.action: User navigates to /profile/987 — a cold profile that has not been read recently.

steps.title: LB forwards to a web replica
steps.action: Identical routing as the hot path.

steps.title: Web tier checks Redis
steps.action: Handler tries the cache as always — it does not yet know the key is absent.

steps.title: Redis returns nil (MISS)
steps.action: The key isn't present (never read, or evicted by LRU, or expired). Redis responds with nil in ~0.5ms.
steps.decision: MISS — fall through to DB read replica

steps.title: Web tier queries the read replica
steps.action: Read traffic is routed by the connection-pool driver to a replica, not the primary, to protect write capacity.
steps.codeOrCommand:
SELECT id, name, bio, updated_at
FROM users
WHERE id = 987;
-- routed to read replica via replica-aware driver

steps.title: Web tier backfills Redis (fire-and-forget)
steps.action: The row is written to Redis with a 10-minute TTL. This is dispatched in parallel with the response — it does not block the user.

steps.title: Web tier serializes the response
steps.action: Assembles the 200 response from the DB row (not waiting on the Redis backfill).

steps.title: LB relays the response
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Browser renders the page
steps.action: Total cold-path latency ~20–35ms — a few times slower than a hot hit, but still well inside the budget. The NEXT request for this profile will be hot.

operations.title: Write request (UPDATE + cache invalidation)
operations.name: Write request (UPDATE + cache invalidation)
operations.description: POST /api/profile/42 with a new bio. Web tier UPDATEs the primary, deletes the cache key, and returns. The next read takes a miss and re-warms from the primary.

steps.title: User submits an edited profile
steps.action: User edits their bio in the web UI and clicks Save. The browser POSTs a JSON body to the API.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /api/profile/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Content-Type: application/json
Cookie: session=abc123 {"bio": "First computer programmer."}

steps.title: LB forwards to a web replica
steps.action: POSTs are not sticky at this layer — any replica can handle them.

steps.title: Web tier validates input and issues the UPDATE
steps.action: Handler authenticates the session, confirms the session user matches the profile id, validates field length, and issues a single UPDATE against the primary.

payload.stmt: UPDATE users SET bio = $1, updated_at = now WHERE id = $2

steps.title: Primary commits the write
steps.action: Primary writes the new row, flushes WAL (fsync), and acknowledges. Replicas will pick up the change over the streaming replication connection within ~50–200ms.

payload.stmt: UPDATE users SET bio = $1, updated_at = now WHERE id = $2

steps.title: Web tier invalidates the Redis key (DEL, not SET)
steps.action: The web tier sends a DEL for `profile:42` so the next reader takes a miss and pulls the fresh row. DEL is preferred over write-through SET because the read replica may lag briefly — forcing the miss onto the primary keeps reads consistent with the just-committed write.
steps.note: The next read handler should route to the primary (not a replica) for ~1s after a write by this user, to avoid reading stale data from a lagging replica. Implementations use a short 'read-your-writes' window keyed on user id.

steps.title: Web tier returns 200
steps.action: Response body confirms the new bio. The CDN is not involved because this is an API (dynamic) response, not a cached static asset.

steps.title: LB relays the response
steps.action: Return path.

steps.title: Client shows the updated profile
steps.action: End-to-end write latency typically 15–40ms. The client usually updates its local state optimistically and reconciles on the 200 — making the perceived latency effectively zero.

tradeoffs.chosen: Move sessions out of the web tier into a shared store (Redis or NoSQL)
tradeoffs.rationale: Sticky sessions work until an instance dies; shared sessions let any server handle any request, which is the prerequisite for autoscaling and rolling deploys.

tradeoffs.chosen: Master-replica SQL rather than jumping straight to NoSQL
tradeoffs.rationale: A 10:1 read/write ratio is served beautifully by replicas plus a cache, and you keep transactional writes. NoSQL is the right move only once the master can no longer absorb writes.

tradeoffs.chosen: Message queue + worker fleet instead of threads inside the web process
tradeoffs.rationale: Long-running jobs inside the request process couple user latency to worker health and make autoscaling math awkward; a queue lets web and workers scale on independent signals.

tradeoffs.chosen: CDN in front of object storage
tradeoffs.rationale: Serving images from the app tier wastes egress and CPU, and never benefits from edge caching. The CDN is almost free compared to the bandwidth it saves.

tradeoffs.chosen: Active-passive with async replication before active-active
tradeoffs.rationale: Active-active needs conflict resolution and careful write routing; active-passive gives you DR with far less complexity and is sufficient until a single region is provably saturated.

tradeoffs.chosen: Shard by user id only after vertical scaling + replicas are exhausted
tradeoffs.rationale: Sharding pays a permanent complexity tax (cross-shard joins, rebalancing). Deferring it until the data really does not fit on one master keeps the codebase simple for longer.
